---
title: Formatting
description: >
  Format documents with Panache and see how it lays out Markdown, tables, math,
  and code.
---

Panache makes your Markdown source easier to read and keeps formatting
consistent across your project. It preserves your document's meaning. Once
you've formatted a document, running Panache again produces the same output.

## Using the Formatter

### Format and Check Files

Format a document in place, or give Panache a directory to format the supported
files inside it:

```sh
panache format document.qmd
panache format docs/
```

To check formatting without writing changes:

```sh
panache format --check .
```

When files need formatting, `--check` exits with a nonzero status. Whether you
format or check, Panache follows your project's configuration and respects its
file exclusions. See [Configuration](configure.qmd).

To pipe a document through Panache, use `--stdin-filename` to give it a
filename. Panache uses that name to choose the Markdown flavor, reads from
standard input, and writes the formatted result to standard output:

```sh
panache --stdin-filename=document.qmd format <document.qmd
```

See [Editor Setup](lsp.qmd) to format documents as you edit and
[Integrations](integrations.qmd) to use Panache with CI, pre-commit, and dprint.

### Choose a Wrapping Mode

By default, Panache wraps paragraphs to a line width of 80 columns. Put your
project's preferences in `panache.toml`:

```toml
[format]
line-width = 80
wrap = "reflow"
```

Choose a wrapping mode to suit how you write:

  | Mode       | Behavior                                              |
  | ---------- | ----------------------------------------------------- |
  | `reflow`   | Rewrap paragraphs to fit `line-width`.                |
  | `preserve` | Keep existing line breaks.                            |
  | `sentence` | Put each sentence on its own line.                    |
  | `semantic` | Keep line breaks and add a break after each sentence. |

The `sentence` and `semantic` modes don't limit line length. When finding
sentence boundaries, Panache takes common abbreviations and your document's
language into account. See [Sentence-Wrapping
Abbreviations](../reference/configuration.qmd#no-break-abbreviations) to
customize which abbreviations it recognizes.

For a single run, you can override a setting on the command line:

```sh
panache format -o wrap=sentence document.qmd
```

The [configuration reference](../reference/configuration.qmd#formatting-style)
lists all formatting options and their defaults.

### Format Embedded Code

Panache formats code fences and their attributes. To format the code inside them
as well, configure an external formatter and make sure its command is available
on your `PATH`. See [Configure Linting and Embedded
Code](configure.qmd#configure-linting-and-embedded-code) for setup and the
[formatter presets](../reference/formatter-presets.qmd) for supported tools.

### Ignore Directives

Use HTML comments to leave the formatting in part of your document untouched.
This is useful for ASCII diagrams or other content whose spacing matters:

```markdown
<!-- panache-ignore-format-start -->
This    paragraph   has    custom     spacing
that  will   be   preserved   exactly.
<!-- panache-ignore-format-end -->
```

To turn off both formatting and linting for part of a document, use
`<!-- panache-ignore-start -->` and `<!-- panache-ignore-end -->` instead.

## Formatting Examples

These examples use Panache's default settings for Quarto documents unless they
specify another setting or Markdown flavor. Panache uses consistent markers,
clear indentation, and spacing to make your document's structure easy to see in
the source. Some features, such as definition lists and fenced divs, require a
[flavor](../reference/configuration.qmd#flavor) that supports them.

### Text Wrapping

Panache wraps paragraphs to `line-width`. Here's how a paragraph looks with
`line-width = 60`:

Input

:   ```markdown
    Panache wraps paragraphs to make the source easier to read and keeps related words together. You can choose a different wrapping mode for your project.
    ```

Output

:   ```markdown
    Panache wraps paragraphs to make the source easier to read
    and keeps related words together. You can choose a different
    wrapping mode for your project.
    ```

Panache preserves hard line breaks in every wrapping mode. It writes them as a
backslash at the end of the line, which is easier to see than two trailing
spaces.

### Headings

Panache writes headings with `#`, `##`, and so on (ATX headings). It removes
decorative hashes at the end and adds blank lines around each heading. It also
separates attributes with a single space. In Pandoc, Quarto, and R Markdown, it
expands the `{-}` shorthand to the heading attribute `{.unnumbered}`.

Input

:   ```markdown
    Introduction
    ============
    Text

    ##  Results  ##

    ### Details{.important  .highlight }
    ```

Output

:   ```markdown
    # Introduction

    Text

    ## Results

    ### Details {.important .highlight}
    ```

### Emphasis and Strong

Panache uses asterisks for emphasis and strong emphasis:

Input

:   ```markdown
    An _important_ point and a __strong__ claim.
    ```

Output

:   ```markdown
    An *important* point and a **strong** claim.
    ```

Panache may escape literal emphasis markers so they stay as text when the
document is read as Markdown again.

### Code

Panache uses enough backticks to enclose inline code, even when the code itself
contains backticks. For code blocks, it uses backtick fences, puts the language
first, and encloses any other attributes in braces. Indented code blocks become
fenced blocks.

Input

:   ````markdown
    ``` {.haskell .numberLines}
    qsort [] = []
    ```
    ````

Output

:   ````markdown
    ```haskell {.numberLines}
    qsort [] = []
    ```
    ````

Tabs become spaces by default. To keep tabs in code, set
[`tab-stops = "preserve"`](../reference/configuration.qmd#tab-stops).

### Lists

Bullet lists use `-`, with two spaces of indentation for each nesting level.
Panache removes blank lines between items when each item contains just one
paragraph.

In CommonMark, you can put a list marker on a line of its own. Once that item
contains a block of content, later blocks stay in the item if they have the
indentation that item requires, even after a blank line.

In CommonMark and GitHub-Flavored Markdown (GFM), a nested ordered list can
start at any number if it immediately follows a heading or horizontal rule. If
it follows paragraph text, it must start at `1` or have a blank line before it.
A nested list marker with no content stays part of the current paragraph.

CommonMark and GFM also allow an HTML block immediately after a list marker.
When Panache adjusts the list's indentation, it keeps the raw HTML and its
relative indentation.

Input

:   ```markdown
    * Item 1
      + Nested item
          *  Deeply nested
     +  Item 2
    ```

Output

:   ```markdown
    - Item 1
      - Nested item
        - Deeply nested
    - Item 2
    ```

Panache keeps your numbering style in ordered and fancy lists and aligns
continuation lines with the text after the list marker. Task lists use `- [ ]`
and `- [x]` for both top-level and nested tasks. If your Markdown parser
requires four spaces of indentation for each nesting level, enable the
[`four-space-rule`](../reference/configuration.qmd#lists) extension.

#### Definition Lists

Each definition starts with `:` followed by three spaces. When a definition
contains several blocks, Panache separates them with blank lines and indents
continuation blocks by four spaces.

Tables and HTML comments stay inside the definition they belong to, including in
Hugo documents. Panache adjusts the indentation of HTML that continues a
definition so that later blocks remain in the same definition.

Input

:   ```markdown
    Term
    : Definition
    ```

Output

:   ```markdown
    Term
    :   Definition
    ```

### Block Quotes

Each line in a block quote starts with `>`, followed by a space. Paragraphs
inside the quote follow the chosen wrapping mode.

Panache keeps the blank line between a list and a block quote that follows it.
To put a quote inside a list item, indent its `>` markers to line up with the
item's text.

In CommonMark and GFM, a quote ends the list item if it's indented less than the
item's text, even without a blank line. Inside a list item, Panache also keeps
the blank line between a quote and a following paragraph so the paragraph stays
outside the quote.

Input

:   ```markdown
    >This is a block quote. This
    >paragraph has two lines.
    ```

Output

:   ```markdown
    > This is a block quote. This paragraph has two lines.
    ```

### Tables

Panache formats pipe, grid, simple, and multiline tables. By default, it indents
pipe, simple, and multiline tables by two spaces. Set
[`table-indent = 0`](../reference/configuration.qmd#table-indentation) to keep
them at the left margin. Grid tables stay at the left margin so Pandoc
recognizes them as tables.

For multiline tables, Panache finds cell boundaries using the column positions
after tabs have been expanded. When inline code is joined onto a single line,
Panache removes any continuation lines in the row that this leaves empty, even
with `wrap = "preserve"`.

#### Pipe Tables

Panache adds padding to show each column's alignment in the source and removes
excess padding. In Pandoc-based flavors, the number of dashes in the separator
row can control the relative widths of the rendered columns. Panache keeps those
dash counts when they affect the layout.

When Pandoc reads a table, it uses these proportions only if a source row is
longer than its configured width (72 columns by default). Panache keeps enough
padding to stay above that threshold.

Input

:   ```markdown
    | Right | Left | Default | Center|
    |------:|:-----|---------|:------:|
    | 12  |  12  |    12   |    12  |
    |  123  |  123 |   123   |   123  |
    |  1  |    1 |     1   |     1 |
    ```

Output

:   ```markdown
      | Right | Left | Default | Center |
      | ----: | :--- | ------- | :----: |
      |    12 | 12   | 12      |   12   |
      |   123 | 123  | 123     |  123   |
      |     1 | 1    | 1       |   1    |
    ```

#### Grid Tables

Panache wraps prose within the existing columns. It keeps column widths because
Pandoc uses them to determine the rendered layout. Lists, code, and other block
content inside cells keep their structure.

Input

:   ```markdown
    +--------------------+--------+
    | Description        | Value  |
    +====================+========+
    | First              | 12     |
    | sample.            |        |
    |                    |        |
    +--------------------+--------+
    ```

Output

:   ```markdown
    +--------------------+--------+
    | Description        | Value  |
    +====================+========+
    | First sample.      | 12     |
    +--------------------+--------+
    ```

#### Simple Tables

Panache sizes columns to fit their contents and aligns cell text according to
the header. It moves captions below the table and prefixes them with `:`.

Input

:   ```markdown
       Right     Left     Center     Default
     -------     ------ ----------   ---------------
          12       12      12            12
       123       123       123          123
           1     1        1             1

       :  A caption
    ```

Output

:   ```markdown
        Right Left    Center  Default
      ------- ------ -------- ---------
           12 12        12    12
          123 123      123    123
            1 1         1     1

      : A caption
    ```

#### Multiline Tables

Panache wraps prose within the existing column widths and removes extra blank
lines between rows. It keeps the widths because they affect the rendered layout.
Code spans, links, and math stay intact when cells wrap. Panache uses the
original column positions to read the text in each cell before it adjusts
punctuation or whitespace.

Input

:   ```markdown
    -------------------------------------------------------------
     Centered   Default           Right Left
      Header    Aligned         Aligned Aligned
    ----------- ------- --------------- -------------------------
      First     row              12.0   Example of a row that
                                        spans multiple lines.


      Second    row                 5.0 Here's another one. Note
                                        the blank line between
                                        rows.
    -------------------------------------------------------------
    ```

Output

:   ```markdown
      -------------------------------------------------------------
       Centered   Default           Right Left
        Header    Aligned         Aligned Aligned
      ----------- ------- --------------- -------------------------
         First    row                12.0 Example of a row that
                                          spans multiple lines.

        Second    row                 5.0 Here's another one. Note
                                          the blank line between
                                          rows.
      -------------------------------------------------------------
    ```

### Math

Panache adds spaces around operators and keeps subscripts and superscripts next
to the terms they apply to. In display math, it indents the contents of
environments, aligns columns at `&` markers, and lines up row endings so the
source is easier to follow.

Input

:   ```markdown
    $$
    \begin{aligned}
    x _1&=a+b\\
    x _{12}&=2a+b\\
    y&=a-b
    \end{aligned}
    $$
    ```

Output

:   ```markdown
    $$
      \begin{aligned}
        x_1    & = a + b  \\
        x_{12} & = 2a + b \\
        y      & = a - b
      \end{aligned}
    $$
    ```

By default, Panache wraps long display equations at relation signs and operators
to fit `line-width`. Content after a multiline environment starts on a new line
at the display's indentation level. Subscripts, superscripts, and punctuation
stay attached to the environment's closing marker.

Use `math = "preserve"` to keep your line breaks, or `math = "verbatim"` to
leave the math content untouched. Panache also leaves malformed math untouched,
along with any command arguments it can't interpret. See [Math
Formatting](../reference/configuration.qmd#math-formatting) for modes, delimiter
styles, and indentation settings.

### Links

Panache keeps link text and destinations as they are. It normalizes spacing and
quotation marks around titles and attributes.

Input

:   ```markdown
    [Panache](https://panache.bz/  'Project website')
    ```

Output

:   ```markdown
    [Panache](https://panache.bz/ "Project website")
    ```

### Fenced Divs

Fenced divs group content between lines of colons. Panache normalizes their
attributes and removes blank lines at the start and end of their content. A
nested div uses two more colons than its parent, so you can tell their
boundaries apart.

Input

:   ```markdown
    ::: Warning ::::::
    This is a warning.

    ::: Danger
    This is a warning within a warning.
    :::
    ::::::::::::::::::
    ```

Output

:   ```markdown
    ::: Warning
    This is a warning.

    ::::: Danger
    This is a warning within a warning.
    :::::
    :::
    ```

### MyST Directives

In the MyST flavor, Panache formats directive options and separates them from
the body with a blank line. It formats Markdown content in directives it
recognizes, such as admonitions and figures.

Panache leaves the bodies of unknown directives as you've written them. It also
preserves literal content, such as code, math, and `eval-rst` blocks, and keeps
each `toctree` entry on its own line. Literal content keeps its internal
indentation, as well as any indentation from the directive's opening fence, even
inside lists and block quotes.

For fenced code within Markdown bodies, Panache preserves lines that contain
only whitespace. If a code block has no closing fence, Panache keeps its content
and indentation. It lengthens directive fences when needed to enclose formatted
code blocks or nested directives, keeping the opening and closing fences the
same length.

Input

:   ````markdown
    ```{{code-block}} python
    :caption:   Fibonacci

    def fib(n):
        if n < 2:
            return n
        return fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2)
    ```
    ````

Output

:   ````markdown
    ```{{code-block}} python
    :caption: Fibonacci

    def fib(n):
        if n < 2:
            return n
        return fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2)
    ```
    ````

### Admonitions

To format `!!!` admonitions, enable
[`python-markdown-admonitions`](../reference/configuration.qmd#admonitions). For
collapsible `???` and `???+` blocks, enable `pymdownx-details`. Panache indents
the body by four spaces and formats it like ordinary content.

Input

:   ```markdown
    !!! note "Heads up"

        Read the introduction
        before running the examples.
    ```

Output

:   ```markdown
    !!! note "Heads up"
        Read the introduction before running the examples.
    ```

### Footnotes

Footnote text follows your chosen wrapping mode. Panache indents continuation
blocks by four spaces, as in list items.

Input

:   ```markdown
    A claim.[^note]

    [^note]: Supporting evidence appears
        in the appendix.
    ```

Output

:   ```markdown
    A claim.[^note]

    [^note]: Supporting evidence appears in the appendix.
    ```

### Horizontal Rules {#horizontal-rulers}

Horizontal rules use hyphens and extend to `line-width`, making section breaks
visible in the source. With `line-width = 40`:

Input

:   ```markdown
    First section.

    ***

    Second section.
    ```

Output

:   ```markdown
    First section.

    ----------------------------------------

    Second section.
    ```

Set `horizontal-rule-style = "compact"` to use `---` instead. Panache adds blank
lines around rules to keep them distinct from heading underlines and metadata
delimiters.

### Blank Lines

Panache reduces multiple blank lines between blocks to one:

Input

:   ```markdown
    Paragraph 1


    Paragraph 2
    ```

Output

:   ```markdown
    Paragraph 1

    Paragraph 2
    ```

### Frontmatter

Panache normalizes YAML spacing and indentation. It wraps prose in plain YAML
values and folded text blocks (`>`) using your document's wrapping mode. Literal
text blocks (`|`) keep their line breaks.

Input

:   ```markdown
    ---
    echo:    false
    list:
    -  a
    -     b
    ---
    Text
    ```

Output

:   ```markdown
    ---
    echo: false
    list:
      - a
      - b
    ---

    Text
    ```

### Chunk Options

In Quarto and R Markdown code chunks, Panache moves simple options from the
header into `#|` comments and formats them as YAML. Options that contain R
expressions stay in the header, even when the expressions contain spaces, as in
`eval = n > 1`.

Input

:   ````markdown
    ```{{r foobar, echo=FALSE, dependson = c("foo", "bar"), fig.cap = "A caption"}}
    a <- 1
    b <- 2
    ```
    ````

Output

:   ````markdown
    ```{{r, dependson=c("foo", "bar")}}
    #| label: foobar
    #| echo: false
    #| fig-cap: "A caption"

    a <- 1
    b <- 2
    ```
    ````

Captions follow your document's wrapping mode. Use a folded YAML text block
(`>-`) for a long caption that should wrap across lines.

## Jupyter Notebooks

Run `panache format notebook.ipynb` to format each Markdown cell independently.
When you pass a directory, Panache finds notebooks automatically and skips
`.ipynb_checkpoints` directories. Use `--check` to check formatting in CI, or
`--stdin-filename notebook.ipynb` to pipe notebook JSON through standard input.

Panache supports notebook format version 4. It changes only the Markdown source
values that need formatting and preserves the rest of the notebook JSON,
including executable code cells, outputs, metadata, IDs, and attachments.
Nonempty Markdown cells end with a newline. You can't lint notebooks or select
line ranges for notebook formatting from the command line.

The `jupyter` flavor uses GFM with JupyterLab math conventions. It recognizes
`$...$`, `$$...$$`, bracket delimiters with doubled backslashes in the Markdown
source, and TeX environments without surrounding math delimiters. Math can span
several nonblank lines, even when those lines look like Markdown blocks. It can
also continue onto later lines within a heading. A blank line ends the math
region. Pipes inside math don't split table cells.

Panache doesn't treat a leading `---` as YAML metadata in this flavor. It also
keeps heading whitespace as you've written it so GFM-style anchor links stay
valid. Use `--flavor jupyter` to apply these rules to standalone Markdown files.
